name: Big O Notation
description: A mathematical notation that describes the upper bound of an algorithm's time or space complexity. It helps compare how algorithms scale as input size grows.
roadmap: Understand what algorithm complexity means and why it matters
Learn the concept of input size 'n' and how it drives performance
Study the common complexity classes: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²)
Practice calculating Big O for simple loops and nested loops
Learn space complexity and how to analyze memory usage
Compare algorithms using Big O to make informed choices
Study best, average, and worst case analysis
Apply Big O analysis to real data structures like arrays and hash tables

name: Sorting Algorithms
description: Methods for arranging elements in a specific order, such as ascending or descending. Common examples include bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort, each with different performance trade-offs.
roadmap: Understand why sorting is a fundamental problem in CS
Implement and trace bubble sort to build intuition
Learn selection sort and insertion sort as simple O(n²) algorithms
Study merge sort as a divide-and-conquer O(n log n) algorithm
Implement quicksort and understand its partitioning strategy
Learn heap sort and how it uses the heap data structure
Compare all algorithms by time complexity, space complexity, and stability
Know which sorting algorithm to choose for a given use case

name: Search Algorithms
description: Techniques for finding specific elements within data structures. Linear search checks every element while binary search efficiently halves the search space on sorted data.
roadmap: Understand what it means to search for an element in a collection
Implement linear search and understand O(n) complexity
Learn why sorted data enables faster searching
Implement binary search and trace through examples
Understand binary search's O(log n) complexity and prove it
Apply binary search to problems beyond simple arrays
Learn about interpolation search as an extension
Practice search problems on coding platforms

name: Graph Algorithms
description: Algorithms that operate on graph data structures to solve problems like finding shortest paths, detecting cycles, and traversing networks. Key examples include BFS, DFS, and Dijkstra's algorithm.
roadmap: Review graph terminology: vertices, edges, directed vs undirected
Implement Breadth-First Search (BFS) using a queue
Implement Depth-First Search (DFS) using recursion or a stack
Use BFS/DFS to detect cycles and connected components
Learn Dijkstra's algorithm for shortest paths in weighted graphs
Study Bellman-Ford for graphs with negative weights
Understand minimum spanning trees with Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms
Practice graph problems on LeetCode and competitive programming sites

name: Dynamic Programming
description: An optimization technique that solves complex problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and storing their solutions. It avoids redundant computation through memoization or tabulation.
roadmap: Understand the two properties: overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure
Solve the Fibonacci sequence recursively, then optimize with memoization
Learn top-down (memoization) vs bottom-up (tabulation) approaches
Solve classic 1D DP problems: coin change, climbing stairs
Tackle 2D DP problems: longest common subsequence, edit distance
Learn the knapsack problem and its variants
Practice identifying DP patterns in new problems
Study interval DP and DP on trees for advanced applications

name: Greedy Algorithms
description: A problem-solving approach that makes the locally optimal choice at each step, hoping to find a global optimum. Works well for problems like activity selection and Huffman coding.
roadmap: Understand what 'greedy choice' means and when it leads to optimal solutions
Study the activity selection problem as a classic greedy example
Implement Huffman coding for data compression
Learn the fractional knapsack problem (greedy vs 0-1 knapsack)
Understand why greedy doesn't always work (use counterexamples)
Compare greedy to dynamic programming approaches
Practice greedy problems involving intervals, scheduling, and graphs
Build intuition for when to apply greedy vs other strategies

name: Divide and Conquer
description: A strategy that breaks a problem into smaller subproblems, solves each independently, and combines their results. Merge sort and quicksort are classic examples of this paradigm.
roadmap: Understand the three-step pattern: divide, conquer, combine
Analyze merge sort as the canonical divide and conquer example
Learn how the Master Theorem helps analyze recursive algorithms
Implement binary search through a divide and conquer lens
Study the closest pair of points algorithm
Implement Strassen's matrix multiplication
Practice identifying problems that have a natural divide structure
Understand the trade-off between recursive overhead and improved complexity

name: Recursion
description: A technique where a function calls itself to solve smaller instances of the same problem. Every recursive solution needs a base case to prevent infinite loops and a recursive case that moves toward it.
roadmap: Understand what the call stack is and how function calls work
Write your first recursive function: factorial
Learn the two essential parts: base case and recursive case
Trace through Fibonacci using recursion
Understand how recursion relates to mathematical induction
Practice tree traversal problems using recursion
Learn how to convert recursion to iteration when needed
Study tail recursion and how compilers optimize it

name: Backtracking
description: A systematic method for exploring all possible solutions by building candidates incrementally and abandoning them when they fail constraints. Used in puzzles like N-Queens and Sudoku solvers.
roadmap: Understand exhaustive search and why it's sometimes necessary
Learn the backtracking template: choose, explore, unchoose
Implement the N-Queens problem step by step
Solve a Sudoku solver using backtracking
Study permutations and combinations generation
Learn pruning techniques to speed up backtracking
Understand the difference between backtracking and brute force
Practice subset-sum and word search problems

name: Hashing
description: A technique that maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values using hash functions. It enables near-constant time lookups and is the backbone of hash tables and data integrity checks.
roadmap: Understand what a hash function does and what makes a good one
Learn the key properties: determinism, uniformity, and fixed output size
Study collision: why it happens and why it's unavoidable
Implement chaining as a collision resolution strategy
Learn open addressing: linear probing and quadratic probing
Understand load factor and when to resize a hash table
Study cryptographic hash functions (MD5, SHA) and their uses
Apply hashing to real problems: deduplication, caching, and checksums

name: A* Search
description: An informed search algorithm that finds the shortest path between nodes using a heuristic to guide exploration. It combines the cost to reach a node with an estimate of the remaining distance to efficiently find optimal paths.
roadmap: Review BFS and Dijkstra's algorithm as uninformed search methods
Understand the concept of a heuristic function h(n)
Learn the A* evaluation function: f(n) = g(n) + h(n)
Implement A* on a grid-based pathfinding problem
Study admissible heuristics and why they guarantee optimality
Learn the Manhattan distance and Euclidean distance as common heuristics
Compare A* performance to BFS and Dijkstra's in practice
Apply A* to game development or robotics path planning

name: Dijkstra's Algorithm
description: A greedy algorithm that finds the shortest paths from a source node to all other nodes in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights. It is widely used in network routing and GPS navigation.
roadmap: Review graph basics: weighted edges and adjacency representations
Understand the single-source shortest path problem
Trace through Dijkstra's algorithm manually on a small graph
Implement Dijkstra's using a priority queue (min-heap)
Analyze the time complexity: O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap
Understand why it doesn't work with negative edge weights
Compare to Bellman-Ford for handling negative weights
Apply Dijkstra's to network routing and map navigation problems

name: Binary Search
description: An efficient algorithm that finds a target value in a sorted array by repeatedly halving the search space. With O(log n) time complexity, it is far faster than linear search for large datasets.
roadmap: Understand the prerequisite: data must be sorted
Trace through binary search by hand on a sorted array
Implement iterative binary search and test edge cases
Implement recursive binary search and compare
Understand why the complexity is O(log n)
Learn off-by-one errors and how to avoid them
Apply binary search to find insertion positions and ranges
Solve advanced problems using binary search on the answer

name: Arrays
description: A fundamental data structure that stores elements in contiguous memory locations, allowing fast access by index. Arrays have fixed size in many languages and offer O(1) random access.
roadmap: Understand how arrays are stored in memory as contiguous blocks
Learn zero-based indexing and how to access elements
Practice common operations: insert, delete, search, and iterate
Understand the time complexity of each array operation
Learn about dynamic arrays and how they resize automatically
Study multi-dimensional arrays (2D arrays for matrices)
Practice common interview problems: two pointers, sliding window
Build a simple project using arrays, like a to-do list

name: Linked Lists
description: A linear data structure where each element (node) contains data and a pointer to the next node. Unlike arrays, linked lists allow efficient insertions and deletions without shifting elements.
roadmap: Understand the node structure: data + pointer to next node
Implement a singly linked list with insert and delete operations
Visualize how pointers chain nodes together
Implement a doubly linked list with prev and next pointers
Practice traversal, reversal, and cycle detection
Understand the trade-offs vs arrays: faster inserts, slower access
Implement common patterns: merging lists and finding the middle
Solve the 'reverse a linked list' problem iteratively and recursively

name: Stacks
description: A last-in, first-out (LIFO) data structure where elements are added and removed from the same end. Stacks are used in function call management, undo operations, and expression evaluation.
roadmap: Understand the LIFO principle with real-world analogies
Implement a stack using an array
Implement a stack using a linked list
Learn the core operations: push, pop, peek, isEmpty
Understand how the call stack uses this structure
Use a stack to balance parentheses in expressions
Implement undo functionality using a stack
Solve next greater element and other monotonic stack problems

name: Queues
description: A first-in, first-out (FIFO) data structure where elements are added at the back and removed from the front. Queues model real-world scenarios like task scheduling and print job management.
roadmap: Understand the FIFO principle with real-world analogies like a line
Implement a queue using an array
Implement a queue using two stacks
Learn circular queues to avoid wasted space
Understand priority queues and how they differ
Use a queue to implement BFS on a graph
Study deques (double-ended queues) and their applications
Implement a task scheduler simulation using a queue

name: Hash Tables
description: A data structure that stores key-value pairs using a hash function to compute an index into an array of buckets. Hash tables provide average O(1) time complexity for lookups, insertions, and deletions.
roadmap: Understand the motivation: O(1) average lookup with a hash function
Learn how a hash function maps keys to bucket indices
Implement a hash table with chaining for collision resolution
Implement open addressing with linear probing
Understand load factor and when to resize the table
Analyze worst-case vs average-case complexity
Study real-world uses: caches, database indexes, and sets
Implement a basic in-memory cache using a hash table

name: Binary Trees
description: A hierarchical data structure where each node has at most two children, called left and right. Binary trees form the basis for more specialized structures like BSTs, heaps, and expression trees.
roadmap: Understand what a tree data structure is and its key terminology
Learn the difference between a general tree and a binary tree
Implement a basic binary tree node class
Practice tree traversals: inorder, preorder, and postorder
Implement BFS (level-order traversal) on a binary tree
Understand balanced vs unbalanced trees and their impact
Study tree height, depth, and diameter calculations
Build a project using binary trees, like an expression parser

name: Heaps
description: A specialized tree-based structure that satisfies the heap property: in a max-heap, every parent is greater than its children. Heaps efficiently support priority queue operations and are used in heap sort.
roadmap: Understand the heap property for both max-heaps and min-heaps
Learn how a binary heap is stored efficiently as an array
Implement insert (heapify-up) and the mechanics of bubbling up
Implement extract-max/min (heapify-down)
Build a complete heap from an unordered array using buildHeap
Implement heap sort using the max-heap
Understand priority queues and how heaps implement them
Apply heaps to the k-largest elements and median maintenance problems

name: Graphs
description: A data structure consisting of vertices (nodes) connected by edges. Graphs can be directed or undirected and model relationships like social networks, maps, and dependency chains.
roadmap: Learn key terminology: vertices, edges, directed vs undirected
Understand weighted vs unweighted graphs
Learn adjacency matrix representation and its trade-offs
Learn adjacency list representation and when to prefer it
Implement a simple graph class with add_vertex and add_edge
Understand connected components, cycles, and paths
Study DAGs (Directed Acyclic Graphs) and topological sort
Model a real problem as a graph (social network or city map)

name: Tries
description: A tree-like data structure used for efficient retrieval of keys in a dataset, typically strings. Each node represents a character, making tries ideal for autocomplete and spell-checking features.
roadmap: Understand the motivation: fast prefix-based string lookups
Learn how each node represents a character in a path
Implement trie insert and search operations
Add an 'end of word' marker to each node
Implement prefix search (startsWith) for autocomplete
Understand time and space complexity compared to hash maps
Implement delete from a trie
Build an autocomplete system or spell-checker using a trie

name: Binary Search Trees
description: A binary tree where the left subtree contains only nodes with smaller values and the right subtree only larger values. BSTs enable efficient searching, insertion, and deletion in O(log n) average time.
roadmap: Review binary trees and understand the BST ordering property
Implement BST insert and trace through examples
Implement BST search and verify O(log n) average case
Implement inorder traversal and observe it produces sorted output
Implement BST delete, handling three cases (leaf, one child, two children)
Understand how an unbalanced BST degrades to O(n)
Learn about self-balancing BSTs: AVL trees and Red-Black trees
Implement a sorted set using a BST

name: Red-Black Trees
description: A self-balancing binary search tree where each node is colored red or black, with rules that guarantee the tree stays approximately balanced. Red-black trees provide O(log n) worst-case performance for all operations.
roadmap: Understand why plain BSTs can become unbalanced and slow
Learn the five red-black tree properties
Understand rotations: left rotation and right rotation
Study the insert fixup procedure and case analysis
Understand the delete fixup procedure
Verify that all operations maintain O(log n) complexity
Compare red-black trees to AVL trees in terms of balance guarantees
Recognize red-black trees in Java's TreeMap and C++ std::map

name: B-Trees
description: A self-balancing search tree optimized for systems that read and write large blocks of data. B-trees keep data sorted and allow searches, insertions, and deletions in O(log n) time, and are widely used in databases and file systems.
roadmap: Understand why binary trees are inefficient for disk-based storage
Learn the concept of order (minimum degree) in a B-tree
Study the B-tree properties: all leaves at same depth, minimum fill
Trace through B-tree search operation
Understand B-tree insert and how nodes split
Understand B-tree delete and how nodes merge
Learn about B+ trees and how they differ from B-trees
Understand how databases use B+ trees for indexes

name: Skip Lists
description: A probabilistic data structure that uses multiple levels of linked lists to allow fast search, insertion, and deletion in O(log n) expected time. Skip lists are an elegant alternative to balanced trees.
roadmap: Review sorted linked lists and their O(n) search limitation
Understand the concept of express lanes with multiple levels
Learn how random coin flips determine node height
Trace through a skip list search operation
Implement skip list insert with randomized level assignment
Implement skip list delete
Analyze expected O(log n) time complexity using probability
Compare skip lists to balanced BSTs: simplicity vs guarantees

name: Bloom Filters
description: A space-efficient probabilistic data structure that tests whether an element is a member of a set. Bloom filters may produce false positives but never false negatives, making them ideal for reducing expensive lookups.
roadmap: Understand the problem: fast set membership with limited memory
Learn how a bloom filter uses a bit array and multiple hash functions
Trace through an insert operation (setting bits)
Trace through a lookup operation (checking bits)
Understand why false positives occur but false negatives don't
Calculate the false positive rate given filter size and hash functions
Learn use cases: web caches, databases, spell checkers
Implement a simple bloom filter from scratch

name: Machine Learning
description: A branch of AI where systems learn patterns from data without being explicitly programmed. ML models improve their performance on tasks through experience and are used in recommendations, predictions, and more.
roadmap: Understand what machine learning is and how it differs from traditional programming
Learn the three main types: supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning
Set up Python with NumPy, Pandas, and scikit-learn
Work through a complete end-to-end ML project with a real dataset
Learn about training/validation/test splits and why they matter
Study overfitting, underfitting, and how to evaluate model performance
Experiment with different algorithms and compare their results
Deploy a simple ML model as a web API

name: Neural Networks
description: Computing systems inspired by biological neural networks in the brain. They consist of layers of interconnected nodes that process information and learn complex patterns from data.
roadmap: Understand the biological inspiration: neurons and synapses
Learn about perceptrons as the simplest neural unit
Study the anatomy of a neural network: input, hidden, and output layers
Understand activation functions: ReLU, sigmoid, and tanh
Learn forward propagation step by step
Understand how backpropagation computes gradients
Implement a small neural network from scratch in Python
Train a network on MNIST or another beginner dataset

name: Deep Learning
description: A subset of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers to learn hierarchical representations of data. Deep learning powers breakthroughs in image recognition, language processing, and game playing.
roadmap: Ensure a solid understanding of basic neural networks and backpropagation
Set up a deep learning environment with PyTorch or TensorFlow
Understand why depth matters: hierarchical feature learning
Train your first deep network on an image classification task
Learn about common architectures: CNNs, RNNs, and Transformers
Understand regularization techniques: dropout, batch normalization
Study transfer learning and fine-tuning pretrained models
Build and deploy a deep learning model on a practical problem

name: Natural Language Processing
description: The field of AI focused on enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language. NLP powers chatbots, translation services, and sentiment analysis tools.
roadmap: Understand core NLP tasks: classification, NER, translation, and summarization
Learn text preprocessing: tokenization, stemming, and lemmatization
Study word representations: bag-of-words, TF-IDF, and word embeddings
Work with pre-trained word embeddings like Word2Vec and GloVe
Learn sequence models: RNNs and LSTMs for text
Study the Transformer architecture and attention mechanism
Use Hugging Face to fine-tune a BERT-based model
Build a practical NLP application: sentiment analyzer or chatbot

name: Computer Vision
description: A field of AI that trains computers to interpret and understand visual information from images and videos. Applications include facial recognition, autonomous vehicles, and medical image analysis.
roadmap: Understand how images are represented as pixel arrays
Learn basic image operations: filtering, edge detection, and transforms
Study convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and how they process images
Implement image classification with a pretrained CNN
Learn object detection architectures: YOLO and Faster R-CNN
Study image segmentation techniques
Understand data augmentation for training robust models
Build a computer vision project: face detection or object counter

name: Reinforcement Learning
description: A type of machine learning where an agent learns to make decisions by receiving rewards or penalties for its actions. It powers game-playing AIs and robotic control systems.
roadmap: Understand the agent-environment interaction loop
Learn key concepts: state, action, reward, and policy
Study the Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework
Implement a simple Q-learning agent on a gridworld
Learn about exploration vs exploitation trade-off
Study Deep Q-Networks (DQN) combining RL and deep learning
Train an agent on an OpenAI Gym environment
Understand policy gradient methods and actor-critic algorithms

name: Supervised Learning
description: A machine learning approach where models are trained on labeled data, learning to map inputs to known outputs. Common tasks include classification (spam detection) and regression (price prediction).
roadmap: Understand what labeled data is and how it enables learning
Learn the difference between classification and regression
Implement linear regression and understand the loss function
Implement logistic regression for binary classification
Learn how to evaluate models: accuracy, precision, recall, F1
Study overfitting and use cross-validation to prevent it
Explore ensemble methods: random forests and gradient boosting
Apply supervised learning to a real dataset end-to-end

name: Unsupervised Learning
description: A machine learning approach where models find hidden patterns in data without labeled examples. Techniques include clustering similar items together and reducing data dimensionality.
roadmap: Understand why we sometimes have data without labels
Learn K-means clustering and implement it from scratch
Study hierarchical clustering and dendrogram visualization
Learn dimensionality reduction with PCA
Understand t-SNE for high-dimensional data visualization
Study anomaly detection as an unsupervised problem
Apply clustering to a real dataset for customer segmentation
Compare supervised vs unsupervised approaches for the same problem

name: Decision Trees
description: A supervised learning model that makes predictions by learning a series of if-then rules from data features. Decision trees are intuitive, interpretable, and form the basis of powerful ensemble methods like random forests.
roadmap: Understand how a decision tree makes predictions via if-then rules
Learn splitting criteria: Gini impurity and information gain
Implement a decision tree from scratch using a greedy algorithm
Visualize a trained decision tree to understand its decisions
Understand overfitting and how pruning helps
Learn about random forests as an ensemble of decision trees
Study gradient boosted trees (XGBoost, LightGBM)
Apply decision trees to a classification problem and interpret the results

name: Clustering
description: An unsupervised learning technique that groups similar data points together based on their features. Popular algorithms like K-means and DBSCAN are used in customer segmentation and anomaly detection.
roadmap: Understand what clustering is and when to use it
Learn distance metrics: Euclidean, cosine, and Manhattan distance
Implement K-means and understand the convergence process
Use the elbow method to choose the number of clusters
Learn DBSCAN for density-based clustering
Understand cluster evaluation metrics: silhouette score
Visualize clusters using dimensionality reduction
Apply clustering to a real dataset and interpret the groups

name: Transformer Architecture
description: A neural network architecture that relies entirely on attention mechanisms to process sequential data. Transformers revolutionized NLP and are the foundation for models like GPT, BERT, and most modern AI systems.
roadmap: Understand the limitations of RNNs that transformers were designed to solve
Learn self-attention: how each token attends to every other token
Study multi-head attention and why multiple heads help
Understand positional encodings and why they are needed
Learn the encoder and decoder stacks
Study layer normalization and residual connections
Implement a simplified transformer in PyTorch
Understand how BERT (encoder-only) and GPT (decoder-only) differ

name: Large Language Models
description: Massive neural networks trained on vast text corpora that can generate, summarize, translate, and reason about language. LLMs like GPT-4 and Claude are transforming how software interacts with human knowledge.
roadmap: Understand transformer architecture as the foundation of LLMs
Learn about pretraining on next-token prediction
Study tokenization: BPE and WordPiece algorithms
Understand scaling laws: how model size affects capability
Learn about RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback)
Study in-context learning and how prompts guide model behavior
Understand hallucination and how to mitigate it
Interact with LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic) and build a simple application

name: Prompt Engineering
description: The practice of designing and refining input prompts to guide large language models toward desired outputs. Good prompt engineering can dramatically improve the quality and relevance of AI-generated responses.
roadmap: Understand how LLMs process and respond to text prompts
Learn zero-shot prompting: asking directly without examples
Study few-shot prompting: providing examples in the prompt
Learn chain-of-thought prompting for complex reasoning tasks
Understand role prompting and system message design
Practice output formatting: asking for JSON, lists, or specific structures
Study prompt injection attacks and safety considerations
Build a practical tool using prompt engineering techniques

name: Fine-Tuning
description: The process of taking a pretrained model and further training it on a smaller domain-specific dataset. Fine-tuning allows models to specialize for particular tasks without training from scratch.
roadmap: Understand the concept of pretrained models and feature reuse
Learn the difference between fine-tuning and training from scratch
Set up a fine-tuning pipeline using Hugging Face Transformers
Understand learning rate selection for fine-tuning
Study full fine-tuning vs parameter-efficient methods (LoRA, adapters)
Learn about catastrophic forgetting and how to mitigate it
Fine-tune a model on a classification or generation task
Evaluate and compare fine-tuned vs base model performance

name: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
description: A technique that enhances language model responses by retrieving relevant documents from a knowledge base before generating an answer. RAG reduces hallucinations and keeps models grounded in factual information.
roadmap: Understand why LLMs hallucinate and how retrieval helps
Learn what embeddings are and how they enable semantic search
Set up a vector database (Chroma, Pinecone, or Weaviate)
Implement document chunking and embedding storage
Build a basic retrieval pipeline: embed query, find nearest chunks
Combine retrieval with an LLM using a prompt template
Evaluate RAG quality: relevance, faithfulness, and completeness
Build a full RAG chatbot over a custom document collection

name: Embeddings
description: Numerical vector representations of text, images, or other data that capture semantic meaning in a high-dimensional space. Similar items have similar embeddings, enabling semantic search, clustering, and classification.
roadmap: Understand why raw text can't be used directly by ML models
Learn about word embeddings: Word2Vec and GloVe
Understand how embeddings capture semantic similarity
Study sentence and document embeddings (SBERT, OpenAI embeddings)
Learn cosine similarity as the standard distance metric
Implement a semantic search engine using embeddings
Understand how embeddings power recommendation systems
Explore multimodal embeddings that combine text and images

name: Attention Mechanism
description: A neural network component that allows models to focus on relevant parts of an input sequence when producing an output. Attention was originally introduced for machine translation and became the core of the Transformer architecture.
roadmap: Understand the problem attention was designed to solve in sequence-to-sequence models
Learn about encoder-decoder attention and alignment
Study the query, key, value framework
Understand scaled dot-product attention mathematically
Learn multi-head attention and its benefits
Understand self-attention and how each token attends to others
Visualize attention weights to understand what models focus on
Study how attention is used in cross-modal models (vision-language)

name: Generative AI
description: A class of AI models that can generate new content such as text, images, audio, and video. Generative AI includes large language models, diffusion models, and GANs, and is rapidly changing creative and knowledge work.
roadmap: Understand the distinction between discriminative and generative models
Learn about the major categories: LLMs, diffusion models, and GANs
Experiment with text generation using the OpenAI or Anthropic API
Explore image generation with Stable Diffusion or DALL-E
Study the capabilities and limitations of current generative models
Learn about content moderation and safety in generative AI
Build a simple generative AI application
Follow current research and understand where the field is heading

name: AI Ethics
description: The study of the moral implications of building and deploying AI systems. It covers fairness, transparency, privacy, accountability, and the societal impact of automated decision-making.
roadmap: Understand why ethics matters in AI system design
Learn about algorithmic bias and how training data shapes outcomes
Study real-world examples of AI failures and their consequences
Understand fairness metrics: demographic parity, equal opportunity
Learn about model explainability and interpretability techniques
Study data privacy concerns and regulations like GDPR
Understand AI safety research and alignment problems
Develop a framework for ethical AI review in your own projects

name: AI Agents
description: AI systems that can autonomously perceive their environment, make decisions, and take actions to accomplish goals. Modern AI agents combine LLMs with tools like web search, code execution, and external APIs.
roadmap: Understand what makes an AI agent different from a simple model
Learn the ReAct pattern: reason and act in interleaved steps
Study tool use: giving an LLM access to functions and APIs
Implement a simple agent with web search and calculator tools
Learn about memory: short-term context vs long-term storage
Study multi-agent systems and how agents collaborate
Understand agent evaluation: task success rate and efficiency
Build an autonomous agent that completes a multi-step task

name: Diffusion Models
description: A class of generative models that learn to reverse a gradual noising process to create new data. Diffusion models produce state-of-the-art results in image generation and are the backbone of Stable Diffusion and DALL-E.
roadmap: Understand generative modeling and the goal of learning a data distribution
Learn the forward diffusion process: gradually adding noise to data
Understand the reverse diffusion process: learning to denoise
Study the math behind diffusion: score matching and denoising objectives
Learn about U-Net architectures used in diffusion models
Understand classifier-free guidance for conditioned generation
Explore latent diffusion models and how they work in the latent space
Experiment with Stable Diffusion via Hugging Face Diffusers library

name: Transfer Learning
description: A machine learning technique where a model trained on one task is reused as the starting point for a model on a different but related task. Transfer learning dramatically reduces training time and data requirements.
roadmap: Understand the intuition: knowledge from one task transfers to another
Learn about pretrained models and where to find them (Hugging Face, timm)
Study feature extraction: using a frozen pretrained model as a backbone
Understand fine-tuning: updating pretrained weights on new data
Learn when to freeze vs unfreeze layers
Apply transfer learning to image classification with a ResNet
Apply transfer learning to NLP with BERT
Compare transfer learning vs training from scratch on a small dataset

name: Convolutional Neural Networks
description: A class of deep learning models designed specifically for processing grid-like data such as images. CNNs use convolutional layers to automatically learn spatial hierarchies of features, from edges to objects.
roadmap: Understand why fully connected networks are inefficient for images
Learn what a convolutional filter does and how it slides over an image
Understand feature maps and how they represent learned patterns
Study pooling layers: max pooling and average pooling
Learn common CNN architectures: LeNet, VGG, ResNet
Implement a CNN in PyTorch or TensorFlow for image classification
Understand skip connections in ResNet and why they help training
Fine-tune a pretrained CNN on a custom image dataset

name: Recurrent Neural Networks
description: A class of neural networks designed for sequential data where outputs depend on previous computations. RNNs maintain a hidden state that captures information from earlier in the sequence, though they struggle with long-range dependencies.
roadmap: Understand why feedforward networks cannot handle sequences naturally
Learn how RNNs maintain a hidden state across time steps
Understand backpropagation through time (BPTT)
Study the vanishing gradient problem in deep RNNs
Learn LSTMs and how gates solve the vanishing gradient problem
Study GRUs as a simpler alternative to LSTMs
Implement a character-level language model with an RNN
Understand when Transformers have replaced RNNs in practice

name: Gradient Descent
description: An optimization algorithm that iteratively updates model parameters in the direction that minimizes a loss function. Gradient descent and its variants are the primary training method for virtually all modern neural networks.
roadmap: Understand what a loss function measures and why we minimize it
Learn the concept of a gradient as the direction of steepest ascent
Implement batch gradient descent for a simple linear regression
Understand the learning rate and how it affects convergence
Learn stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and mini-batch SGD
Study momentum-based optimizers: SGD with momentum
Learn adaptive optimizers: AdaGrad, RMSProp, and Adam
Understand learning rate schedules and warm-up strategies

name: Operating Systems
description: Software that manages computer hardware and provides services for running applications. Operating systems handle memory, processes, file systems, and device communication.
roadmap: Understand what an OS is and why it is needed
Learn the difference between kernel space and user space
Study process management: creation, states, and context switching
Understand memory management: virtual memory and paging
Learn about file systems and how data is organized on disk
Study I/O management and device drivers
Understand synchronization: mutexes, semaphores, and condition variables
Read the first few chapters of the OSTEP textbook (free online)

name: Compilers
description: Programs that translate source code written in a high-level language into machine code that a computer can execute. Compilers perform lexical analysis, parsing, optimization, and code generation.
roadmap: Understand the phases of compilation: scanning, parsing, analysis, optimization, codegen
Learn about lexical analysis and how a scanner tokenizes source code
Study context-free grammars and how parsers use them
Implement a simple recursive descent parser
Learn about abstract syntax trees (ASTs)
Understand semantic analysis: type checking and symbol tables
Study common compiler optimizations: constant folding, inlining
Build a tiny language compiler or transpiler as a capstone project

name: Memory Management
description: The process of controlling and coordinating computer memory, including allocation, deallocation, and organization. Concepts include virtual memory, paging, and garbage collection.
roadmap: Understand the memory hierarchy: registers, cache, RAM, and disk
Learn about heap vs stack memory allocation
Study manual memory management: malloc and free in C
Understand common bugs: memory leaks, dangling pointers, buffer overflows
Learn about virtual memory and address translation
Study paging and page tables
Understand garbage collection algorithms: mark-and-sweep, reference counting
Explore how garbage collectors work in Java, Python, and Go

name: Process Scheduling
description: The method by which an operating system decides which process gets CPU time and for how long. Scheduling algorithms like round-robin and priority-based scheduling balance fairness and efficiency.
roadmap: Understand the CPU scheduler's role in multitasking
Learn about process states: ready, running, blocked, and terminated
Study First Come First Serve (FCFS) scheduling
Learn Shortest Job First (SJF) and its preemptive variant
Implement Round Robin scheduling and understand time quantum
Study priority scheduling and potential for starvation
Understand multilevel feedback queues used in real OSes
Compare scheduling algorithms on example process sets

name: File Systems
description: The way an operating system organizes, stores, and retrieves data on storage devices. File systems manage directories, permissions, and metadata to keep data accessible and structured.
roadmap: Understand why file systems are needed over raw disk storage
Learn about inodes and how files are tracked in Unix systems
Study directory structures and path resolution
Understand file permissions and access control
Learn about disk layout: blocks, sectors, and clusters
Study journaling file systems and crash recovery
Understand virtual file systems (VFS) as an abstraction layer
Compare ext4, NTFS, and APFS as real-world examples

name: Virtual Machines
description: Software emulations of physical computers that run operating systems and applications in isolation. VMs enable running multiple OS instances on a single host and are fundamental to cloud computing.
roadmap: Understand the motivation for virtualization: isolation and resource sharing
Learn about Type 1 (bare-metal) and Type 2 (hosted) hypervisors
Study CPU virtualization techniques: trap-and-emulate
Understand memory virtualization and shadow page tables
Learn I/O virtualization and device passthrough
Compare VMs to containers as lighter-weight alternatives
Set up a VM locally using VirtualBox or VMware
Understand how cloud providers like AWS and Azure use VMs

name: Distributed Systems
description: Systems where components on networked computers communicate and coordinate to achieve a common goal. Key challenges include consistency, availability, and partition tolerance (the CAP theorem).
roadmap: Understand why distributed systems are complex: failures, latency, partial state
Learn about the CAP theorem and its implications
Study consistency models: strong, eventual, and causal consistency
Understand distributed consensus with the Raft or Paxos algorithm
Learn about distributed transactions and two-phase commit
Study distributed storage: replication strategies and quorums
Understand message queues and event-driven architecture
Take MIT 6.824 (Distributed Systems) course lectures online

name: Concurrency
description: The ability of a system to handle multiple tasks at the same time through threads, processes, or asynchronous execution. Concurrency introduces challenges like race conditions and deadlocks.
roadmap: Understand the difference between concurrency and parallelism
Learn about threads and how they share memory within a process
Understand race conditions and why shared mutable state is dangerous
Learn mutexes (locks) to protect critical sections
Study semaphores and condition variables for coordination
Understand deadlock: causes, conditions, and prevention
Learn lock-free data structures and compare-and-swap (CAS)
Study the actor model and message passing as an alternative to shared memory

name: CPU Architecture
description: The design and organization of a computer's central processing unit, including instruction sets, registers, and pipelines. Understanding CPU architecture helps explain how software executes at the hardware level.
roadmap: Understand the fetch-decode-execute cycle
Learn about registers and the role of the ALU
Study instruction set architectures (ISA): x86 vs ARM
Understand pipelining and instruction-level parallelism
Learn about cache hierarchy: L1, L2, L3 and cache coherence
Study branch prediction and speculative execution
Understand RISC vs CISC design philosophies
Write simple assembly code to see how high-level code maps to instructions

name: Containers / Docker
description: A lightweight virtualization technology that packages applications and their dependencies into isolated environments called containers. Docker is the most widely used container runtime, enabling consistent deployments across development and production.
roadmap: Understand what containers are and how they differ from VMs
Install Docker and run your first container
Learn Docker concepts: images, containers, volumes, and networks
Write a Dockerfile to containerize a simple application
Build and run a multi-container app using Docker Compose
Learn about container registries and pushing to Docker Hub
Understand container networking and port mapping
Explore best practices: minimal base images and layer caching

name: Kubernetes
description: An open-source container orchestration system that automates deploying, scaling, and managing containerized applications. Kubernetes is the industry standard for running containers in production at scale.
roadmap: Understand why container orchestration is needed at scale
Learn the Kubernetes architecture: control plane and worker nodes
Study core objects: Pods, Deployments, Services, and ConfigMaps
Set up a local cluster with Minikube or kind
Deploy a containerized application and expose it as a Service
Learn about scaling with ReplicaSets and Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
Understand rolling updates and rollbacks
Study namespaces, resource limits, and RBAC for multi-tenant clusters

name: Microservices
description: An architectural style that structures an application as a collection of small, independently deployable services that communicate over a network. Microservices enable teams to develop, deploy, and scale components independently.
roadmap: Understand monolithic architecture and its limitations at scale
Learn the microservices principles: single responsibility and loose coupling
Study service communication: REST, gRPC, and message queues
Understand service discovery and how services find each other
Learn about API gateways as a single entry point
Study distributed tracing and centralized logging for observability
Understand the challenges: distributed transactions, data consistency
Build a small system with two or three communicating services

name: HTML/CSS
description: The foundational technologies of the web. HTML provides the structure and content of web pages, while CSS controls their visual presentation, layout, and styling.
roadmap: Learn basic HTML: tags, attributes, and document structure
Understand semantic HTML: headers, articles, sections, and nav
Learn CSS selectors: element, class, ID, and pseudo-selectors
Study the box model: margin, border, padding, and content
Learn Flexbox for one-dimensional layouts
Learn CSS Grid for two-dimensional layouts
Understand responsive design with media queries
Build a personal portfolio page to practice everything

name: JavaScript
description: The programming language of the web that enables interactive and dynamic content in browsers. JavaScript runs on both client and server sides and powers modern web applications.
roadmap: Learn variables, data types, and control flow
Understand functions, scope, and closures
Study the DOM API and how to manipulate HTML elements
Learn about events and event-driven programming
Understand asynchronous JS: callbacks, Promises, and async/await
Study ES6+ features: arrow functions, destructuring, and modules
Learn about the JavaScript event loop and how async code works
Build a small interactive project: todo app or weather widget

name: HTTP Protocol
description: The application-layer protocol used for transmitting web resources like HTML pages. HTTP defines how messages are formatted and transmitted, and how servers and browsers respond to requests.
roadmap: Understand the client-server model and how HTTP fits in
Learn about HTTP methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, and PATCH
Study HTTP status codes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error
Understand HTTP headers: content type, authorization, and caching
Learn the difference between HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2
Understand HTTPS and how TLS secures HTTP connections
Study cookies and sessions for state management
Use browser dev tools to inspect real HTTP requests

name: REST APIs
description: An architectural style for designing networked applications using standard HTTP methods. REST APIs use endpoints and JSON data to enable communication between frontend clients and backend servers.
roadmap: Understand what an API is and why REST is popular
Learn REST constraints: statelessness, uniform interface, and layered system
Study resource naming conventions and URL design
Implement CRUD operations with appropriate HTTP methods and status codes
Learn about request and response bodies in JSON
Understand authentication in REST APIs: API keys and JWT
Learn API versioning strategies
Build and document a simple REST API

name: Frontend Frameworks
description: Libraries and frameworks like React, Vue, and Angular that simplify building interactive user interfaces. They provide component-based architecture, state management, and efficient DOM updates.
roadmap: Understand why frameworks exist: virtual DOM and component reuse
Learn React basics: JSX, components, and props
Understand state management with useState and useEffect hooks
Build a multi-component app and manage data flow
Learn routing with React Router for single-page applications
Study global state management with Context API or Zustand
Understand server-side rendering and Next.js App Router
Deploy a React application to Vercel or Netlify

name: Backend Development
description: The server-side of web applications that handles business logic, database operations, and API endpoints. Backend technologies include Node.js, Python, and various frameworks for building robust server applications.
roadmap: Choose a backend language and framework: Node.js/Express or Python/FastAPI
Understand server concepts: request handling, middleware, and routing
Build a basic REST API with CRUD endpoints
Connect your API to a database (PostgreSQL or MongoDB)
Implement user authentication with JWTs
Learn error handling and input validation best practices
Understand environment variables and configuration management
Deploy your backend to a cloud service like Railway or Render

name: Web Security
description: Practices and techniques for protecting web applications from threats like XSS, CSRF, and SQL injection. Web security covers input validation, authentication, HTTPS, and secure coding practices.
roadmap: Understand the OWASP Top 10 web vulnerabilities
Learn about Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and how to prevent it
Study SQL injection attacks and how parameterized queries prevent them
Understand Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) and CSRF tokens
Learn about Content Security Policy (CSP) headers
Study HTTPS, TLS, and secure cookie attributes
Understand authentication security: password hashing and token storage
Run a security audit on a sample application

name: Responsive Design
description: An approach to web design that makes pages render well on all device sizes, from phones to desktops. It uses flexible grids, media queries, and fluid images to adapt layouts automatically.
roadmap: Understand why responsive design is essential for mobile users
Learn the viewport meta tag and how it affects rendering
Study CSS media queries to target different screen sizes
Use relative units: %, em, rem, vw, and vh
Implement a mobile-first design approach
Learn Flexbox and Grid for responsive layouts
Test your design on different devices using browser dev tools
Build a landing page that works well on mobile, tablet, and desktop

name: Web Performance
description: The practice of making websites load and run faster through optimization techniques. Key strategies include code splitting, lazy loading, caching, image optimization, and minimizing network requests.
roadmap: Understand Core Web Vitals: LCP, FID, and CLS
Learn how to use Lighthouse and browser dev tools for audits
Optimize images: modern formats (WebP), compression, and lazy loading
Learn about browser caching and cache-control headers
Study code splitting and dynamic imports to reduce bundle size
Minimize blocking scripts and defer non-critical JavaScript
Understand CDNs and how they reduce latency
Apply optimizations to a real site and measure the improvement

name: WebSockets
description: A communication protocol that provides full-duplex communication channels over a single TCP connection. WebSockets enable real-time features like live chat, notifications, and collaborative editing in web applications.
roadmap: Understand the limitations of HTTP for real-time communication
Learn the WebSocket handshake and how the upgrade happens
Understand the WebSocket frame format
Implement a simple WebSocket server using Node.js (ws library)
Build a client that connects and exchanges messages
Study Socket.IO as an abstraction over WebSockets with fallbacks
Build a real-time chat application
Understand when to use WebSockets vs Server-Sent Events vs polling

name: GraphQL
description: A query language for APIs and a runtime for executing those queries that allows clients to request exactly the data they need. GraphQL reduces over-fetching and under-fetching problems common with REST APIs.
roadmap: Understand the problems with REST APIs that GraphQL solves
Learn the GraphQL schema definition language (SDL)
Study the three operation types: query, mutation, and subscription
Implement a GraphQL server with resolvers
Learn about the N+1 query problem and how DataLoader solves it
Understand fragments and how clients compose queries
Study GraphQL subscriptions for real-time data
Build a full-stack app with a GraphQL API

name: Server-Side Rendering
description: A technique where HTML is generated on the server for each request, delivering fully rendered pages to the browser. SSR improves initial page load performance and SEO compared to purely client-side rendering.
roadmap: Understand the difference between CSR, SSR, and SSG
Learn why SSR matters for SEO and initial load performance
Study the trade-offs: server load, time to first byte, and hydration
Implement SSR with Next.js using the App Router
Understand streaming SSR and React Server Components
Learn about incremental static regeneration (ISR)
Study the hydration process and common pitfalls
Deploy an SSR application and measure performance improvements

name: WebAssembly
description: A binary instruction format that runs in the browser at near-native speed. WebAssembly allows code written in languages like C, C++, and Rust to run on the web, enabling high-performance applications.
roadmap: Understand what WebAssembly is and the problem it solves
Learn the WebAssembly text format (WAT) as human-readable Wasm
Understand the compilation pipeline: source language to Wasm
Compile a C or Rust program to WebAssembly using Emscripten or wasm-pack
Learn the WebAssembly JavaScript API for loading modules
Study the memory model and how JS and Wasm share memory
Understand WASI for running WebAssembly outside the browser
Build a performance-critical browser feature using WebAssembly

name: TCP/IP
description: The fundamental communication protocol suite of the internet that defines how data is packaged, addressed, transmitted, and received. TCP ensures reliable delivery while IP handles addressing and routing.
roadmap: Understand the four layers of the TCP/IP model
Learn IP addressing: IPv4 notation and subnetting basics
Understand how routers use IP addresses to forward packets
Learn TCP's three-way handshake for connection establishment
Study TCP reliability features: acknowledgments, retransmission, and flow control
Understand UDP and when to choose it over TCP
Learn about ports and how they distinguish services on one IP
Use Wireshark to capture and analyze real TCP/IP traffic

name: DNS
description: The Domain Name System translates human-readable domain names (like google.com) into IP addresses that computers use to communicate. DNS is often called the phonebook of the internet.
roadmap: Understand why we need DNS: humans use names, computers use IPs
Learn the DNS hierarchy: root, TLD, and authoritative nameservers
Trace a full DNS resolution from stub resolver to authoritative server
Understand DNS record types: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, and TXT
Learn about DNS caching and TTL
Understand DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT)
Study common DNS attacks: cache poisoning and DNS hijacking
Use dig and nslookup to query DNS records yourself

name: Routing
description: The process of selecting paths in a network along which to send data packets. Routers use protocols like OSPF and BGP to determine the best path for data to travel between networks.
roadmap: Understand routers as devices that forward packets between networks
Learn static routing and how routing tables work
Study dynamic routing protocols and their purposes
Learn OSPF as a link-state interior gateway protocol
Understand BGP as the routing protocol of the internet
Study routing metrics: hop count, bandwidth, and latency
Learn about CIDR notation and route aggregation
Use traceroute to observe the hops packets take in real networks

name: Network Security
description: Policies and practices designed to protect the integrity and usability of network infrastructure. It encompasses firewalls, intrusion detection systems, VPNs, and network monitoring.
roadmap: Understand common network threats: eavesdropping, spoofing, and DDoS
Learn about defense in depth as a security strategy
Study firewalls: stateful inspection and rules configuration
Understand intrusion detection systems (IDS) and intrusion prevention systems (IPS)
Learn about VPNs for encrypting traffic over untrusted networks
Study network segmentation and DMZ architectures
Understand network monitoring tools: NetFlow and SNMP
Set up a simple network monitoring solution

name: Firewalls
description: Network security devices that monitor and filter incoming and outgoing traffic based on predefined rules. Firewalls act as a barrier between trusted internal networks and untrusted external networks.
roadmap: Understand what a firewall does and what it cannot do
Learn about packet filtering and stateless firewalls
Study stateful inspection firewalls and connection tracking
Understand application-layer (Layer 7) firewalls
Learn how to write basic firewall rules (allow/deny)
Study default-deny vs default-allow policies
Understand next-generation firewalls (NGFW) and their features
Configure a basic firewall using iptables or UFW

name: OSI Model
description: A conceptual framework with seven layers that standardizes how different network protocols interact. The layers range from physical transmission (Layer 1) to application-level protocols (Layer 7).
roadmap: Understand why layered models help manage network complexity
Learn the seven layers from physical to application
Map common protocols to their OSI layers
Understand encapsulation: how data gets wrapped as it moves down the stack
Study where different network devices operate (switches at Layer 2, routers at Layer 3)
Learn how troubleshooting follows the OSI layers
Compare OSI to the simpler TCP/IP model
Use the OSI model as a framework for diagnosing network problems

name: Wireless Networks
description: Networks that use radio waves instead of physical cables to connect devices. Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and cellular networks are common examples, each with different range and bandwidth characteristics.
roadmap: Understand how radio waves carry data
Learn Wi-Fi standards: 802.11a/b/g/n/ac/ax (Wi-Fi 6)
Understand frequency bands: 2.4 GHz vs 5 GHz trade-offs
Study wireless security protocols: WEP, WPA2, and WPA3
Learn about Bluetooth and its use cases
Understand cellular networks: 4G LTE and 5G basics
Study wireless interference sources and mitigation
Set up and secure a home or office wireless network

name: Load Balancing
description: The practice of distributing network traffic across multiple servers to ensure no single server is overwhelmed. Load balancers improve application availability, reliability, and response times.
roadmap: Understand the problem: single servers become bottlenecks
Learn about Layer 4 (transport) vs Layer 7 (application) load balancing
Study load balancing algorithms: round robin, least connections, IP hash
Understand health checks and how balancers route around failures
Learn about sticky sessions and when they are needed
Study horizontal scaling and how load balancing enables it
Understand global load balancing with GeoDNS and anycast
Configure a load balancer using NGINX or HAProxy

name: Sockets
description: Endpoints for sending and receiving data across a network. Sockets provide the low-level programming interface for network communication using protocols like TCP and UDP.
roadmap: Understand what a socket is: an endpoint for network communication
Learn the socket API: socket, bind, listen, accept, and connect
Implement a simple TCP echo server
Implement a client that connects to the echo server
Understand non-blocking sockets and the select/poll API
Learn about UDP sockets for connectionless communication
Study socket options: timeouts, keep-alive, and reuse
Build a simple HTTP server from scratch using sockets

name: HTTP/2
description: The second major version of the HTTP protocol that introduces multiplexing, header compression, and server push to dramatically improve web performance. HTTP/2 allows multiple requests over a single connection.
roadmap: Review HTTP/1.1 and understand its performance bottlenecks
Learn about head-of-line blocking in HTTP/1.1
Understand HTTP/2 multiplexing: multiple streams over one connection
Study HPACK header compression and why it matters
Learn about server push and its use cases
Understand the binary framing layer replacing text-based messages
Compare HTTP/2 performance improvements with benchmarks
Study HTTP/3 (QUIC) as the next evolution

name: gRPC
description: A high-performance remote procedure call framework developed by Google that uses Protocol Buffers for serialization and HTTP/2 for transport. gRPC is widely used for efficient microservice communication.
roadmap: Understand RPC concepts and how they differ from REST
Learn Protocol Buffers (protobuf) for schema definition and serialization
Install the gRPC tools and generate code from a .proto file
Implement a simple unary gRPC service
Study server-side and client-side streaming
Understand bidirectional streaming for real-time communication
Learn about gRPC interceptors for middleware patterns
Compare gRPC vs REST APIs for microservice communication

name: CDN
description: A Content Delivery Network is a distributed system of servers that delivers web content to users based on their geographic location. CDNs cache content at edge servers worldwide to reduce latency and improve load times.
roadmap: Understand why geographic distance causes latency
Learn how a CDN caches content at edge servers worldwide
Study cache-control headers that CDNs use to determine TTL
Understand the difference between static and dynamic CDN content
Learn about CDN purging and cache invalidation
Study CDN security features: DDoS protection and WAF
Configure a simple CDN using Cloudflare
Measure latency improvements before and after using a CDN

name: VPN
description: A Virtual Private Network creates an encrypted tunnel between a device and a remote server, masking the user's IP and protecting traffic on untrusted networks. VPNs are essential tools for remote access and privacy.
roadmap: Understand what problem VPNs solve: privacy and secure access
Learn how tunneling protocols create encrypted connections
Study VPN protocols: OpenVPN, WireGuard, and IPSec
Understand split tunneling and full tunneling
Learn about site-to-site VPNs for connecting company networks
Understand the role of VPNs in zero-trust network architectures
Set up a WireGuard VPN server on a cloud instance
Understand the limitations and trust model of commercial VPN services

name: Cryptography
description: The science of securing information by transforming it into an unreadable format using mathematical algorithms. Cryptography ensures confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity of data.
roadmap: Understand the three security goals: confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity
Learn about symmetric encryption: AES and its modes
Study asymmetric encryption: RSA and elliptic curve cryptography
Understand hash functions and their properties
Learn about digital signatures and how they prove authenticity
Study key exchange protocols: Diffie-Hellman
Understand TLS and how cryptographic primitives combine in practice
Take the Khan Academy cryptography course for a solid foundation

name: Encryption
description: The process of converting plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and a key, so only authorized parties can read it. Symmetric encryption uses one key, while asymmetric uses a public-private key pair.
roadmap: Understand the basic concept: plaintext + key = ciphertext
Learn symmetric encryption and AES as the modern standard
Understand block ciphers and modes of operation (CBC, GCM)
Study asymmetric encryption: public and private keys
Learn about RSA encryption and decryption at a conceptual level
Understand hybrid encryption: use asymmetric to exchange symmetric keys
Learn about end-to-end encryption and where it is used
Implement encryption in your language of choice using a cryptography library

name: Authentication
description: The process of verifying the identity of a user, device, or system. Common methods include passwords, multi-factor authentication, biometrics, and token-based systems like OAuth.
roadmap: Understand the difference between authentication and authorization
Learn about password-based authentication and why passwords must be hashed
Study password hashing: bcrypt, Argon2, and scrypt
Understand session-based authentication with cookies
Learn token-based authentication with JSON Web Tokens (JWT)
Study multi-factor authentication (MFA) and TOTP
Learn about OAuth 2.0 for delegated authorization
Implement authentication in a web application from scratch

name: Access Control
description: Security techniques that regulate who can view or use resources in a computing environment. Models include role-based access control (RBAC), discretionary access control, and mandatory access control.
roadmap: Understand the principle of least privilege
Learn about discretionary access control (DAC) and Unix file permissions
Study role-based access control (RBAC) and how to model permissions
Understand attribute-based access control (ABAC) for fine-grained policies
Learn about access control lists (ACLs)
Understand mandatory access control (MAC) in systems like SELinux
Study authorization in web applications: middleware and guards
Implement RBAC in a web application

name: Penetration Testing
description: A simulated cyberattack against a system to identify exploitable vulnerabilities before malicious actors do. Pen testing involves reconnaissance, exploitation, and reporting to improve security posture.
roadmap: Understand the legal and ethical framework for penetration testing
Learn the pen testing methodology: reconnaissance, scanning, exploitation, reporting
Set up a safe practice environment using Kali Linux and vulnerable VMs
Study network scanning with Nmap
Learn about web application vulnerabilities using OWASP WebGoat
Understand Metasploit for exploitation
Study privilege escalation techniques
Practice on platforms like Hack The Box or TryHackMe

name: Malware Analysis
description: The process of studying malicious software to understand its behavior, origin, and impact. Analysts use static and dynamic techniques to dissect viruses, trojans, ransomware, and other threats.
roadmap: Understand the malware categories: viruses, worms, trojans, ransomware
Learn static analysis: examining code without executing it
Study tools: strings, objdump, and Ghidra for disassembly
Learn dynamic analysis: running malware in a controlled sandbox
Set up a safe analysis environment with isolated VMs
Study common malware behaviors: persistence, C2 communication, evasion
Practice on real malware samples from VirusTotal or MalwareBazaar
Write an analysis report documenting your findings

name: Network Security Fundamentals
description: Core principles for protecting data during transmission across networks. Topics include encryption in transit, VPNs, secure protocols like TLS, and defense-in-depth strategies.
roadmap: Understand common network attacks: MITM, eavesdropping, replay attacks
Learn how TLS secures data in transit
Study certificate validation and how to detect invalid certificates
Understand VPNs for secure remote access
Learn about network segmentation and VLANs
Study intrusion detection and prevention systems
Understand security monitoring: logs, SIEM, and alerts
Conduct a basic network security audit

name: Secure Coding
description: The practice of writing software that is resistant to security vulnerabilities. It involves input validation, proper error handling, avoiding common pitfalls like buffer overflows, and following security guidelines.
roadmap: Study the OWASP Top 10 as a foundation for common vulnerabilities
Learn input validation: never trust user-supplied data
Understand SQL injection and parameterized query prevention
Study cross-site scripting (XSS) and output encoding
Learn about secure error handling: avoid leaking information
Understand dependency management and keeping libraries updated
Learn security headers and their role in defense in depth
Perform a security review on your own code using a checklist

name: Public Key Infrastructure
description: A framework for managing digital certificates and public-key encryption to enable secure communication. PKI uses certificate authorities, digital signatures, and trust chains to verify identities online.
roadmap: Understand the core problem: how do you trust a public key?
Learn about digital certificates and what information they contain
Study certificate authorities (CAs) and root trust stores
Understand the certificate chain from root to leaf
Learn how certificate signing requests (CSRs) work
Study certificate revocation: CRL and OCSP
Understand Let's Encrypt and how free TLS certificates work
Set up TLS for a web server using your own certificates

name: OAuth
description: An open authorization framework that allows third-party applications to access user resources without exposing credentials. OAuth 2.0 is the industry standard for delegated access and powers 'Login with Google' flows.
roadmap: Understand the problem OAuth solves: delegating access without sharing passwords
Learn the four OAuth 2.0 grant types: authorization code, implicit, client credentials, password
Trace through the Authorization Code flow step by step
Understand access tokens, refresh tokens, and their lifetimes
Learn about scopes for limiting what an application can access
Study OpenID Connect (OIDC) as an identity layer on top of OAuth
Implement OAuth login (Google or GitHub) in a web application
Understand common OAuth security pitfalls: token leakage and redirect URI validation

name: JWT
description: JSON Web Tokens are a compact, URL-safe format for representing claims between two parties. JWTs are widely used for stateless authentication in web APIs and single-page applications.
roadmap: Understand why stateless authentication is useful for APIs
Learn the JWT structure: header, payload, and signature
Understand how the signature ensures integrity
Learn to create and verify JWTs in your language of choice
Study the standard claims: iss, sub, exp, and iat
Understand the difference between signing (JWS) and encryption (JWE)
Learn where to store JWTs securely in a browser
Study common JWT vulnerabilities: alg:none and weak secrets

name: Zero Trust
description: A security model based on the principle 'never trust, always verify.' Zero trust assumes no user or device is inherently trusted, requiring continuous verification regardless of network location.
roadmap: Understand the traditional perimeter security model and its weaknesses
Learn the core zero trust principles: verify explicitly, least privilege, assume breach
Study identity as the new security perimeter
Understand multi-factor authentication in a zero trust context
Learn about micro-segmentation and limiting lateral movement
Study device trust: health checks before granting access
Understand zero trust network access (ZTNA) vs traditional VPNs
Map a zero trust architecture for a real or hypothetical organization

name: CORS
description: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing is a browser security mechanism that controls how web pages request resources from different origins. CORS prevents malicious websites from making unauthorized API calls on behalf of users.
roadmap: Understand the same-origin policy and why browsers enforce it
Learn what constitutes an origin: scheme, host, and port
Understand simple requests vs preflight requests
Learn the key CORS headers: Access-Control-Allow-Origin and others
Study wildcard origins vs specific allowed origins
Understand credentialed requests and cookies across origins
Configure CORS correctly on a backend API
Diagnose and fix common CORS errors in development

name: SQL
description: Structured Query Language is the standard language for managing and querying relational databases. SQL lets you create tables, insert data, and retrieve information using declarative statements.
roadmap: Learn basic SELECT queries with WHERE, ORDER BY, and LIMIT
Understand INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE for data manipulation
Study CREATE TABLE with data types and constraints
Learn JOIN operations: INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL OUTER
Understand GROUP BY and aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG
Learn about subqueries and CTEs (Common Table Expressions)
Study indexes and when to add them for performance
Build a small database for a real project (blog or inventory)

name: Relational Databases
description: Database systems that organize data into tables with rows and columns, linked by relationships through keys. Examples include PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite, all accessed using SQL.
roadmap: Understand the relational model: tables, rows, columns, and keys
Learn about primary keys and foreign keys
Study referential integrity and constraints
Set up PostgreSQL and connect via psql or a GUI like DBeaver
Design a multi-table schema with proper relationships
Learn about JOINs as the primary way to query related tables
Understand ACID properties and why they matter
Build a backend application with a relational database

name: NoSQL
description: A category of databases that store data in formats other than traditional relational tables. Types include document stores (MongoDB), key-value stores (Redis), and graph databases (Neo4j).
roadmap: Understand why NoSQL databases were created and what problems they solve
Learn the four main NoSQL types: document, key-value, column-family, and graph
Set up MongoDB and explore document-based data modeling
Understand embedding vs referencing documents in MongoDB
Learn Redis as a key-value store and cache
Understand eventual consistency and when it is acceptable
Study the CAP theorem in the context of NoSQL databases
Choose the right NoSQL database for a given use case

name: Database Indexing
description: A technique that creates additional data structures to speed up data retrieval operations on database tables. Indexes work like a book's index, allowing the database to find rows without scanning every record.
roadmap: Understand why full table scans are slow for large tables
Learn how a B-tree index organizes data for fast lookups
Create indexes in PostgreSQL and analyze query plans with EXPLAIN
Understand single-column vs composite indexes
Learn about covering indexes and index-only scans
Study when NOT to add an index (write overhead trade-off)
Understand hash indexes and when they outperform B-trees
Optimize a slow query by analyzing and adding the right index

name: Transactions
description: A sequence of database operations that are treated as a single unit of work, following ACID properties. Transactions ensure data consistency even when operations fail or multiple users access data simultaneously.
roadmap: Understand the ACID properties: atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability
Learn the basic transaction commands: BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK
Understand isolation levels: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE
Study concurrency anomalies: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads
Learn about locking mechanisms: shared locks and exclusive locks
Understand optimistic vs pessimistic concurrency control
Study deadlocks in databases and how to prevent them
Implement a bank transfer using transactions to ensure correctness

name: Normalization
description: The process of organizing database tables to reduce data redundancy and improve data integrity. Normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF) provide rules for structuring tables and their relationships.
roadmap: Understand the problems of unnormalized data: anomalies and redundancy
Learn First Normal Form (1NF): atomic values, no repeating groups
Study Second Normal Form (2NF): eliminate partial dependencies
Learn Third Normal Form (3NF): eliminate transitive dependencies
Understand Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)
Practice normalizing a messy unnormalized table to 3NF
Understand when to denormalize for performance
Design a schema from scratch using normalization principles

name: Query Optimization
description: Techniques for improving database query performance by analyzing execution plans and restructuring queries. Optimization involves choosing efficient joins, using indexes, and minimizing data scans.
roadmap: Understand what a query execution plan is and how to read it
Learn to use EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE in PostgreSQL
Identify sequential scans that should be index scans
Understand join algorithms: nested loop, hash join, merge join
Learn query rewriting techniques: avoid SELECT *, use CTEs wisely
Study index usage: covering indexes and partial indexes
Understand statistics and how the query planner makes decisions
Optimize a slow real-world query from start to finish

name: Data Modeling
description: The process of creating a visual representation of a database structure, defining entities, attributes, and relationships. Good data models ensure efficient storage and retrieval of information.
roadmap: Understand conceptual, logical, and physical data models
Learn Entity-Relationship (ER) diagrams and their notation
Identify entities, attributes, and cardinality in a business domain
Convert an ER diagram to a relational schema
Study one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many relationships
Learn junction tables for modeling many-to-many in SQL
Practice modeling a real domain like an e-commerce or library system
Review your schema with normalization principles

name: Database Replication
description: The process of copying and maintaining database data across multiple servers for redundancy and availability. Replication strategies include master-slave, master-master, and multi-region setups.
roadmap: Understand the goals: high availability, disaster recovery, and read scaling
Learn primary-replica (master-slave) replication
Understand synchronous vs asynchronous replication trade-offs
Study replication lag and its implications for reads
Learn multi-primary replication and conflict resolution
Understand logical vs physical replication
Study read replicas for horizontal scaling of read traffic
Set up a PostgreSQL replication pair and test failover

name: Redis
description: An in-memory data structure store used as a database, cache, message broker, and queue. Redis supports rich data types like strings, hashes, lists, sets, and sorted sets with near-instant access times.
roadmap: Understand why in-memory storage is orders of magnitude faster than disk
Install Redis and connect via the redis-cli
Learn the core data types: strings, lists, hashes, sets, and sorted sets
Implement a caching layer using Redis for a database query
Learn about TTL (time-to-live) and cache expiration strategies
Use Redis Pub/Sub for simple message broadcasting
Study Redis persistence options: RDB snapshots and AOF logging
Understand Redis clustering for horizontal scaling

name: CAP Theorem
description: A fundamental theorem in distributed systems stating that a distributed database can guarantee at most two of three properties: Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance. Understanding CAP helps in choosing the right database for a use case.
roadmap: Understand the three properties: Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance
Learn why partition tolerance is unavoidable in real networks
Study CP systems: choose consistency over availability during a partition
Study AP systems: choose availability over consistency during a partition
Understand eventual consistency as a practical middle ground
Learn how different databases position themselves (HBase vs Cassandra)
Explore the PACELC theorem as an extension of CAP
Apply CAP reasoning to choose a database for a specific system design scenario

name: Sharding
description: A database scaling technique that horizontally partitions data across multiple database instances called shards. Each shard holds a subset of the total data, allowing the system to handle more data and traffic than a single machine could.
roadmap: Understand the limits of vertical scaling and why sharding is needed
Learn the difference between horizontal and vertical partitioning
Study common sharding strategies: range-based, hash-based, and directory-based
Understand the challenges: cross-shard queries and hot spots
Learn about consistent hashing to minimize data movement when re-sharding
Study how MongoDB and Cassandra implement sharding
Understand the application-level complexity sharding introduces
Design a sharding strategy for a high-traffic social media feed
